catalog_quote: 2.3 Tones. Kayan Lahta is a tonal language. There are 4 tones in Kayan Lahta and they are contrastive. A glottal is considered as a tone instead of a phoneme as it only occurs with a high tone. It is also called a cut tone. When the tones are changed, the meaning changes also. Low (˩) Mid (˧) High (˥) High glottal (ʔ˥) [p. 27] ... (vii) Every syllable has tone. (not shown in diagram) [p. 30] ... 2.4.2 Minor syllable. There are two types of minor syllable structures: initial nasal, and the first syllable of two-syllable word. [tables: Initial nasal: Nasal [/m/ or /n/ or /ɲ/ or /ŋ/]: /mba˧/ 'shoulder', /ŋqa˥/ 'shave', /ɲwa˧/ 'play'; First syllable of two syllables, [C]ə + syllable: /sə˩nɛ˩/ 'what', /tə˩pi˩/ 'fly', /lə˩kwɛŋ˧/ 'east', /mə˩çɨ˧/ 'friend', /kə˧ sʰə˧/ 'comb', /ə˩pʰi˧/ 'skin'] [p. 31]

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source describes Kayan Lahta as a four-tone language in which every syllable bears tone; disyllables may have a reduced Cə (or syllabic-nasal) minor first syllable before a full syllable (sesquisyllabic shape). It makes no statement about word stress or accent at all; any iambic (minor+major) prominence reading would be an inference from the minor-syllable structure, not a claim of the author.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal distribution gaps only (e.g. /ɨ/ and /ɔ/ do not take the high-glottal tone; /ɘ/ not with low or high-glottal).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology of citation forms; Kaung Htu village variety of Kayan Lahta. Author states tone was not the focus of data collection and breathy phonation was not analysed.
new_statements.identity_note: Ywar 2013 describes Kayan Lahta (ISO 639-3 kvt 'Lahta Karen', Glottolog bookkeeping code laht1236, which Glottolog subsumes under zaye1235 'Lahta-Zayein Karen' [kxk]), specifically the Kaung Htu village variety (southern Shan State); the author notes Lahta varies village to village and is not mutually intelligible with Pekon Kayan (pdu). Zayein proper (kxk) is described only in Shintani 2014 (print, not seen).

new_statements.quote: Analysis of the tonal systems shows that Proto-Kayan retained Luce's Tone Class V, negating Theraphan's (2013) analysis. [...] Kayan dialects show a regular alignment of tones in Tone Class V with Tone Class II, III (Kayan [pdu]) or Tone Class VIII (Geko + Lahta/Zayein). A network analysis of the phonology of 72 lexemes occurring in all doculects shows that there are six clusters within Kayan, and the most divergent cluster is Lahta/Zayein.

It confirms that Lahta/Zayein is tonal (tones assigned by Proto-Karen tone class) and mentions no word stress, which is the same type as the existing Ywar 2013 statement ('tone language, no stress statement'). Whether the body of the paper or slides says anything about stress or minor (sesquisyllabic) syllables is unknown: both PDFs could not be reached by automated download (an automated-access block) on two automated download attempts each (Firefox UA; Chrome UA with referer and Accept headers) and one direct download attempt each. The work is comparative (over 50 Kayan doculects: Geko [ghk], Kayan [pdu], Lahta [kvt], Yinbaw [kvu], Zayein [kxk]), so any st…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The abstract treats the Kayan dialects, including the Lahta/Zayein cluster, as tonal languages whose tones are analysed by Proto-Karen tone class (Lahta/Zayein align Tone Class V with Tone Class VIII); it says nothing about stress, accent or prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog zaye1235 is 'Lahta-Zayein Karen' [kxk]; Glottolog's laht1236 'Lahta Karen' [kvt] is a bookkeeping duplicate that points to it. The existing catalog statement (Ywar 2013) describes the Kaung Htu village variety of Kayan Lahta. Manson 2019 treats 'Lahta/Zayein' as one dialect cluster within the Kayan group (Ethnologue's five codes ghk, pdu, kvt, kvu, kxk), the most divergent of six clusters; its abstract statements are about that cluster, not a single village variety. Manson 2023 is a Karen-wide bibliography and is not about any one variety.

new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the catalog's classification 'tonal' for Kayan Lahta (Ywar 2013: 4 contrastive tones, every syllable has tone) with independent tone data for Lahta (TS) and Zayein (TS) and a reconstructed Proto-Lahta tone box; like Ywar 2013 it makes no word-stress statement, so it neither adds nor contradicts anything on stress. The body of the paper thus matches what the earlier reader inferred from the abstract alone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Comparative-historical handout: Lahta and Zayein are treated as tonal Kayan-cluster varieties whose lexical tones (pitch values per Proto-Karen tone class, with breathy and checked categories) are tabulated and a 'Proto-Lahta' tone box is reconstructed; the only prosodic remark beyond tone is cluster-wide 'variation in articulation/intonation (staccato, flowing stream)'. Nothing is said about word stress, accent or syllable prominence for Lahta/Zayein or any Kayan variety (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/sesquisyllabic/minor syllable = 0 hits in the 10 pp; 'accentology' occurs only in a reference title).
new_statements.identity_note: Manson 2019 treats 'Lahta [kvt]' and 'Zayein [kxk]' as one cluster (9 Lahta/Zayein doculects, tone rows from Shintani's data 'Lahta (TS)', 'Zayein (TS)') within the Kayan cluster of Karenic; Glottolog merges both ISO codes under zaye1235 Lahta-Zayein Karen (laht1236 = bookkeeping). The catalog record rests on Ywar 2013, Kaung Htu village variety of Kayan Lahta, southern Shan State.

sources.note: Nothing. Ch. 2 Phonology (pp. 27-32) states the language is tonal with 4 contrastive tones (low, mid, high, high-glottal), 'Every syllable has tone' (p. 30), and describes minor syllables (syllabic nasal; C+schwa first syllable of disyllables, transcribed with low tone) in sec. 2.4.2 p. 31. The words stress/accent/prominence do not occur anywhere in the thesis; author notes (p. ~150) data collection did not focus on tones.
